title: Title and occasion
short: Naval gunnery practice in the English Channel wakes the dead in a coastal churchyard; dated April 1914, four months before war.
body: The title names firing practice by warships in the English Channel, a regular sound on the Dorset coast near the naval base at Portland. Hardy dated the poem April 1914, at the height of Anglo-German naval rivalry; it was published in May 1914 and collected in Satires of Circumstance (1914), and after August it read as uncannily prophetic. 'Your great guns' addresses the living (and the nation) directly from the grave: the speaker is one of the dead. The poem's mix of ghost-story, comic dialogue and apocalyptic satire is characteristic of Hardy's churchyard poems.

title: Metre and stanza
short: Nine quatrains of iambic tetrameter rhyming abab, a jaunty measure set against an apocalyptic subject.
body: The poem uses cross-rhymed tetrameter quatrains, a measure of hymns and ballads, with frequent enjambment between stanzas ('We thought it was the Judgment-day / And sat upright') which creates a conversational, anecdotal flow. Hardy enjoys comic and feminine rhymes ('hatters / matters', 'wonder / under'), a bathetic register that suits the dead men's grumbling. The last stanza returns to the opening sound of guns, framing the poem and giving it the solemn close the comedy has deferred.

title: chancel window-squares
short: The chancel is the east end of a church around the altar; the 'window-squares' are its glass panes.
body: The chancel (from Latin cancelli, the lattice screen that once divided it from the nave) is the part of the church containing the altar and choir. 'Window-squares' is Hardy's plain, almost rustic compound for panes, here shattered by the concussion of the guns. The detail roots the poem in a real parish church near the coast and sets up the stanza's sacred props, altar-crumb and glebe cow, which are all disturbed together.

anchor: We thought it was the Judgment-day
title: Judgment-day
short: The dead think the guns are the last trumpet of Christian eschatology, at which the dead rise for judgement.
body: Christian tradition holds that at the end of the world a trumpet will sound and the dead will be raised to be judged: 'the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised' (1 Corinthians 15:52; cf. 1 Thessalonians 4:16; Revelation 20:12–13). The dead sit 'upright' in their coffins expecting resurrection, a grotesque and comic picture. The poem later returns to the trumpet in God's own mouth (st. 6), and to the 'judgment-hour', so this mistaken apocalypse frames the whole poem's question about whether any judgement will ever come.

title: drearisome
short: A rare, dialect-flavoured form of 'dreary': dismal, melancholy.
body: 'Drearisome' adds the suffix -some to 'dreary', as in dialect words like 'wearisome' and 'lonesome'; the OED records it as rare. Hardy liked such homely coinages and regionalisms, which ground his metaphysical poems in rural speech. Here it describes the howl of dogs woken by the gunfire, a traditional omen of death; the creatures' reactions (hounds, mouse, worms, cow) form a comic catalogue of the parish disturbed.

anchor: The mouse let fall the altar-crumb
title: the altar-crumb
short: A mouse drops a crumb of the communion bread from the altar: a small comic image with sacramental overtones.
body: The 'altar-crumb' is a fragment of bread left from Holy Communion, which in Christian belief represents or becomes the body of Christ. The mouse nibbling it is a homely detail of a country church, but it also suggests the neglect or debasement of the sacrament in a 'striving' world. The line's companion, 'The worms drew back into the mounds', inverts the usual image of worms feeding on the buried dead: here even they retreat in fear of the supposed Judgement.

title: glebe cow
short: The glebe is land belonging to a parish living; the glebe cow is the parson's cow grazing it.
body: 'Glebe' (Latin gleba, clod, soil) is the portion of land assigned to a parish clergyman as part of his benefice, which he could farm or let; a churchyard and adjoining glebe were often grazed. The cow 'drooled', slavering in alarm or stupidity, a bathetic end to the catalogue of creatures before God's voice cuts in. The word reminds us that the parish is also an economic unit, and anticipates Parson Thirdly's rueful view of his own career.

title: God's speech
short: God himself answers the dead, in a weary, sardonic voice that mocks human warmongering and doubts the Last Judgement will ever come.
body: Hardy, an agnostic, often dramatised a God or a cosmic power who is indifferent, forgetful or ironic (compare 'God-Forgotten' and 'New Year's Eve'). Here God speaks in colloquial idiom ('Mad as hatters', 'Ha, ha'), assures the dead that the noise is only gunnery practice and that 'the world is as it used to be'. His speech, running over four stanzas, condemns nations that 'make / Red war yet redder', yet also casts doubt on his own promises. The irreverence shocked some readers but is central to the poem's satire on Christian nations preparing for war.

title: Mad as hatters
short: A proverbial phrase for complete madness, comically incongruous on God's lips.
body: 'As mad as a hatter' was a common nineteenth-century simile, often linked to the nervous effects of mercury used in felt-hat making, and popularised by the Hatter of Lewis Carroll's Alice books (1865). Placing this colloquialism in the mouth of God undercuts the solemnity expected of the scene. The rhyme 'hatters / matters' and the pun on 'for Christ's sake' (an oath, and literally 'on Christ's behalf') sharpen the point: the warring nations, nominally Christian, do nothing for Christ.

title: scour Hell's floor
short: Comic penance: if this were Judgement, the warmongers would be set to scrub the floor of Hell.
body: 'Scour' means scrub clean, and the image of the belligerent nations doomed to scour Hell's floor is a grotesque domestic punishment, more comic than Dantean. The line break after 'scour' creates a little suspense. The trailing ellipsis after 'threatening' allows God's speech to pause before the joke of 'warmer', which plays on Hell's fire. Some readers find the humour defuses the satire; others see the jocularity as Hardy's way of conveying a deeper bitterness.

title: the trumpet (if indeed / I ever do)
short: God doubts that he will ever sound the last trumpet: the promised Judgement and resurrection may never come.
body: This is the theological sting of the poem. The 'last trump' (1 Corinthians 15:52) is the signal for the general resurrection; God here suggests he may never blow it, because men 'rest eternal sorely need'. 'Rest eternal' echoes the liturgy for the dead ('Requiem aeternam dona eis, Domine', 'Grant them eternal rest, O Lord'). The joke is double-edged: eternal rest is a mercy for exhausted humanity, but it also implies there will be no resurrection and no final justice, a view in keeping with Hardy's agnosticism.

title: indifferent century
short: The dead man's own century, probably the nineteenth, called 'indifferent': mediocre, or religiously lukewarm, or no better than the present.
body: One of the dead wonders whether the world will ever be 'saner' than in the century when 'He sent us under' (killed and buried us). 'Indifferent' can mean mediocre, neither good nor bad, or unconcerned, morally and spiritually lukewarm. Its ambiguity matters: if the dead lived in an 'indifferent' age, the present age of arms races is worse rather than better, undermining any Victorian faith in progress. The line also hints at the cosmic indifference that runs through Hardy's verse.

title: Parson Thirdly
short: A Wessex clergyman from Hardy's fiction; his name suggests sermons divided into firstly, secondly, thirdly.
body: Parson Thirdly is the parson of Weatherbury in Far from the Madding Crowd (1874), set in Hardy's fictional Wessex, where he is a minor, poor and unassuming figure. The name evokes the formal divisions of a long Victorian sermon ('thirdly, my brethren'). His regret that he did not stick 'to pipes and beer' instead of 'preaching forty year' is the poem's comic climax: even the clergy doubt the value of their ministry in a world that never changes. 'Forty year' (the dialect uninflected plural) may glance at the Israelites' forty years in the wilderness (Psalm 95:10).

title: readiness to avenge
short: The guns proclaim nations primed for revenge; written months before August 1914, the line read afterwards as prophecy.
body: The final stanza abandons comedy. The alliterative 'Roaring their readiness' makes the guns animal and eager, and 'to avenge' implies grievances waiting to be paid back, a fitting account of the alliance system and naval arms race of the pre-war years. The phrase gains force from the date: the First World War broke out in August 1914, and the poem's later readers could not hear these lines without that knowledge.

anchor: As far inland as Stourton Tower
title: Stourton Tower
short: King Alfred's Tower, an eighteenth-century folly on the Stourhead estate, commemorating King Alfred's rally against the Danes in 878.
body: Stourton Tower (King Alfred's Tower) is a tall triangular brick folly on the Stourhead estate on the Somerset–Wiltshire border, built for the banker Henry Hoare II in the 1760s–70s to mark the place where Alfred the Great is said to have raised his standard against the Danes. The final lines trace the sound of the guns travelling inland and backward in time: from a monument to a war hero, to the legendary Camelot, to prehistoric Stonehenge. Every site recalls an earlier phase of England's history of war and power, suggesting the long continuity of human conflict.

title: Camelot … Stonehenge
short: Legendary Arthurian court (often placed at Cadbury Castle, Somerset) and the prehistoric monument on Salisbury Plain.
body: Camelot, the court of King Arthur, was identified by the Tudor antiquary John Leland with South Cadbury hill-fort in Somerset, within the region Hardy evokes. Stonehenge, the Neolithic and Bronze Age stone circle in Wiltshire, appears in Tess of the d'Urbervilles as Tess's last refuge. 'Starlit' gives the poem's last image a stillness and timelessness that contrasts with the roaring guns. The receding sequence (Georgian folly, Arthurian legend, prehistory) suggests that war is as old as human civilisation, and that the guns' echo spreads through all of English history.
